brave.title: Rojas v Olson, No. 25-3127 (7th Cir. 2026) :: Justia
brave.snippet:
After entering the United States in 2018 without inspection, Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, a Mexican national, was arrested by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in 2025. Initially, DHS detained him under 8 U.S.C. § 1226, and an immigration judge found he was neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk, ordering his release on bond pending removal.
The district court agreed with DHS’s interpretation and denied the habeas petition, concluding Rojas must be detained pending his removal proceedings. Rojas appealed this decision. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reviewed the case de novo and first found that the appeal was not moot, as DHS had stated its intention to re-detain Rojas if the BIA reversed his bond release.
Because Rojas did not seek admission but applied for forms of relief that do not constitute admission, the court ruled he is not subject to mandatory detention under Section 1225(b)(2)(A). Instead, he falls under Section 1226 and is eligible for a bond hearing. The Seventh Circuit reversed the district court’s denial of habeas relief and remanded with instructions to grant the writ.

A split Seventh Circuit panel rejected President Donald Trump’s stance on mandatory detention for noncitizens apprehended inside the country, making it the sixth federal appeals court to rebuff a legal interpretation central to the administration’s mass-deportation goals.
The government’s argument that noncitizens living in the US are nevertheless “seeking admission” to the country, just like those crossing at the border, doesn’t hold water, wrote Judge Joshua Kolar in Thursday’s opinion . That claim “rests upon the illogical use of both legal fiction and ordinary meaning for the same term,” he said.
For about three decades, including during the Trump’s first term, presidential administrations recognized that noncitizens arrested inside the country were generally entitled to a bond hearing at which they could argue for their release from immigration detention. Such hearings aren’t available to those apprehended while “seeking admission.”
Last year, however, the administration began to interpret the law such that even unauthorized immigrants who have lived in the US for years are “seeking admission” and subject to mandatory detention.
Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, the petitioner in the underlying district court case, “has never applied for anything that counts as ‘admission’ to the United States. Federal circuit courts of appeals are increasingly confronting a significant and evolving question in immigration law: whether a noncitizen who entered the United States without inspection and is later arrested in the interior may be subject to mandatory detention under INA § 235(b)(2)(A), or whether INA § 236(a) applies and makes the noncitizen eligible for an individualized bond hearing before an immigration judge.

Historically, immigration detention law generally distinguished between noncitizens encountered at the border and those arrested inside the United States. For many years, individuals who entered the United States without inspection but were later arrested in the interior were typically placed into proceedings under INA § 236(a), 8 U.S.C. § 1226(a). This provision authorizes the government to arrest and detain a noncitizen pending a decision on whether the person should be removed, but it also permits release on bond or conditional parole. Specifically, § 236(a) provides that, “on a warrant issued by the Attorney General, an alien may be arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States,” and that the government may continue detention or release the person on bond of at least $1,500 or conditional parole.

By contrast, INA § 235(b)(2)(A), 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(2)(A) applies to certain “applicants for admission” and requires mandatory detention. The statute provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained for a proceeding under section 240.” Unlike § 236(a), this provision generally does not provide access to an individualized bond hearing before an immigration judge.

After entering the United States in 2018 without inspection, Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, a Mexican national, was arrested by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in 2025. Initially, DHS detained him under 8 U.S.C. § 1226, and an immigration judge found he was neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk, ordering his release on bond pending removal. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reviewed the case de novo and first found that the appeal was not moot, as DHS had stated its intention to re-detain Rojas if the BIA reversed his bond release.

Instead, he falls under Section 1226 and is eligible for a bond hearing. The Seventh Circuit reversed the district court’s denial of habeas relief and remanded with instructions to grant the writ.
